result:
A deadlock is when two or more threads (or processes, or transactions) each hold a resource the other needs and wait forever for it to be released, so none of them can proceed. The classic case is thread A holding lock 1 and waiting for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1.

It can only happen when four conditions hold at once: resources are exclusive, a thread holds one while waiting for another, a held resource can't be forcibly taken away, and there is a cycle of waiters. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

The most practical fix is to break the cycle by always acquiring locks in the same global order everywhere in the code, for example by sorting on a lock ID or address before taking two of them. Where ordering is hard to enforce, use a lock attempt with a timeout (`tryLock`) and release everything and retry on failure, ideally with a random backoff so the threads don't keep colliding.

Beyond that, hold locks for as short a time as possible, avoid calling unknown code (callbacks, I/O, other modules) while holding one, and prefer a single coarse lock or lock-free designs such as message passing or immutable data when the contention doesn't justify fine-grained locking. Databases handle this differently: they detect the cycle and abort one transaction, so there your job is to retry on a deadlock error.
